title: A Surfactant-Free Palm Oil Cream Base (HAMIN™) for Colloidal Oat (Avena sativa) in Eczema: Formulation, Characterization and In Vivo Evaluation
content: Background/Objectives: Colloidal oat (Avena sativa) is clinically proven in atopic dermatitis (AD), yet the vehicle makes up more than 90% of an oat moisturizer, and conventional bases rely on surfactants that damage the skin barrier. We hypothesized that oat delivered in a surfactant-free palm oil base (HAMIN™) would heal eczematous lesions faster than oat in a surfactant-containing cream. Methods: Nine oil-in-water creams were prepared without any added surfactant following a 32 full factorial design (oat 1, 1.5 and 2% w/w; HAMIN™ 30, 40 and 50% w/w) and characterized for emulsion type, pH, spreadability, rheology, Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectra and 28-day stability. F2 (1% oat) and F8 (2% oat) in 40% HAMIN™ were then evaluated over 14 days in 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene (DNCB)-sensitized mice (n = 5 per group) against a marketed oat cream (colloidal oat in a surfactant-containing base), the HAMIN™ base alone and untreated and normal controls. Results: All creams were smooth, shear-thinning oil-in-water emulsions with pH 5.83–6.19. Spreadability (2.23–4.63 cm) was governed mainly by HAMIN™ concentration (p < 0.001). The lead cream remained physically stable for 28 days, although its pH rose to 7.0–7.2. Both oat–HAMIN™ creams fell from severity grade 3 to grade 1 by Day 14, the 2% cream reaching grade 1 two days ahead of the 1% cream. The base alone, without any oat, also reached grade 1, whereas the marketed oat cream and the untreated lesions both remained crusted at grade 3. Conclusions: With the same active ingredient, the surfactant-free base gave the better therapeutic outcome and contributed more to recovery than the oat concentration did. Removing surfactants from the vehicle is therefore a practical way to raise the performance of established topical actives in eczema, which should be confirmed in adequately powered, blinded studies.
